name: Startup Pitch Exaggeration
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Pitch Deck Problem: Why Startups Oversell Even More Than Incumbents
lesson.summary: Venture-funded quantum computing startups face structural incentives that push their public claims even further ahead of their actual technical state than established players like IBM or Google, making startup announcements the category most worth reading with skepticism.
lesson.body:
IBM and Google are large, publicly traded or publicly accountable companies with quantum computing programs that represent a small fraction of overall revenue, existing alongside decades of other business lines. A quantum computing startup, by contrast, typically has no other product, no other revenue, and often no path to revenue at all except by convincing investors that the underlying technology will eventually be transformative. This difference in structure produces a difference in incentives that shows up directly in the language startups use to describe their progress, and it is worth examining as its own category within the broader catalog of broken promises.

A venture-backed quantum startup typically raises money in rounds, each of which requires convincing new investors that meaningful technical progress has occurred since the last round and that a further, larger opportunity lies just ahead. This creates direct pressure to frame ordinary incremental engineering progress, a small improvement in qubit coherence time, a modest reduction in gate error rates, in the most dramatic language the underlying result can plausibly support. It also creates pressure to lean on the three-to-five-year horizon identified earlier in this unit, since that window is long enough to sound transformative and short enough to justify a new funding round today.

This dynamic is amplified by the technical complexity of the field itself. Evaluating whether a startup's claimed qubit fidelity, error rate, or algorithmic result is actually meaningful requires specialized physics and computer science expertise that most investors, journalists, and potential enterprise customers do not have. This information asymmetry is not unique to quantum computing, it shows up across deep-tech sectors generally, but it is unusually pronounced here because the underlying quantum mechanics genuinely is difficult even for trained scientists outside the specific subfield to evaluate quickly. A claim that sounds impressive to a lay audience may be scientifically modest, or a claim that sounds modest may actually be significant, and the gap between perception and substance is wide enough to be routinely exploited, whether deliberately or through genuine overenthusiasm.

None of this means every quantum computing startup is dishonest. Many are staffed by serious physicists and engineers doing genuine research, and some of the underlying science reported by startups has been independently verified through peer review. The pattern is specifically about the translation layer between the underlying research and the public-facing pitch, where ambiguous or narrow technical results get compressed into broader, more marketable claims, in the same way Google's narrow Sycamore benchmark result got compressed into a broader quantum supremacy narrative in the surrounding coverage.

A useful practical filter, building on the falsifiability principle introduced in the catalog of broken promises chapter, is to ask whether a startup's claim is accompanied by a specific, peer-reviewed technical result with named metrics, such as a stated gate fidelity percentage or a specific algorithm run at a specific problem size, or whether it consists mainly of qualitative language like breakthrough, revolutionary, or game-changing without an attached number. The former is checkable against the growing catalog this unit has been building; the latter is exactly the kind of claim that has historically aged the worst.
